item.title: The midterms are a week away. What do the latest polls say?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The 2026 midterm elections are just 7 days away. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data. The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. And they have been wrong before . Yet time is running out — and the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too. The state-by-state midterm landscape is reaching its final form — and some clear polling trends have emerged. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears. Yahoo The generic congressional ballot Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds). You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading. History is helpful here, courtesy of the RealClear Politics polling average : At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (3 percentage points) on the generic ballot. On Election Day, the GOP translated its final polling lead (also 3 points) into nine seats — enough to flip the House. At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.6 points on the generic ballot. Seven days later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But with 7 days to go, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a Republican polling lead of 2 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House; in 2010, those numbers were 6.9 points and 63 seats, respectively. So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — about 9 percentage points , on average — and it has grown over the last month. Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House. Advantage? Democrats. 12 specific Senate races National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. Here are the 12 races to follow: Maine (Republican seat) Republican Susan Collins (incumbent) Democrat Troy Jackson What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . Two new nonpartisan polls also show Jackson ahead; a Republican poll released over the weekend gives Collins a 0.5% edge. Michigan (Democratic seat) Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress) Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director) What the latest polls say : Ten polls have been conducted in October. Nine of them have shown El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 1 to 7 percentage points . The latest survey (for the Detroit News) puts El-Sayed ahead by 6 points . Ohio (Republican seat) Republican Jon Husted (incumbent) Democrat Sherrod Brown (former senator) What the latest polls say : Brown has edged Husted in nearly every poll conducted since the first week of October, with margins ranging from 2 to 6 percentage points. But a new Echelon Insights poll shows a tie . Georgia (Democratic seat) Democrat Jon Ossoff (incumbent) Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with October polls putting him ahead by an average of 9 percentage points . North Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman) Democrat Roy Cooper (former governor) What the latest polls say : Cooper leads by more than 10 points, on average . One of the most recent nonpartisan surveys showed him ahead by 14 . New Hampshire (Democratic seat) Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator) Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) What the latest polls say : Pappas and Sununu were previously trading leads in polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But Pappas appears to have opened a substantial lead — average margin: 7 percentage points — over the last month. Alaska (Republican seat) Republican Dan Sullivan (incumbent) Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Surveys conducted in October show Peltola leading by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . Some September polls showed a tie, or Sullivan slightly ahead. Iowa (Republican seat) Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress) Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete) What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries . Texas (Republican seat) Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general) Democrat James Talarico (state legislator) What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted this fall has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins are small — between 2 and 6 points. A new YouGov poll gives Talarico a 5-point lead . Nebraska (Republican seat) Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor) Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support) What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent nonpartisan results suggest Osborn could be competitive, and a couple of new Osborn-affiliated polls show Ricketts and his independent challenger trading small leads. Kansas (Republican seat) Republican Roger Marshall (incumbent) Democrat Adam Hamilton (Methodist pastor who previously considered an independent run) What the latest polls say : Marshall leads by 1 point in the latest sounding — but it's the only survey conducted over the last month that shows him ahead. The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points). South Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Darline Graham (incumbent, appointed to replace her brother Lindsey Graham after his death in July) Democrat Annie Andrews (pediatrician and former U.S. House candidate) What the latest polls say : Graham holds a narrow lead in recent surveys . But it is small enough — between 1 and 3 percentage points — that Democrats are now targeting South Carolina as well. A partisan poll released on Thursday gave Andrews a 1-point advantage. Advantage? Democrats. They've been consistently gaining ground over the last month, to the point where they are now favored to flip the Senate — unless the polls are wrong. Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability President Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Greenville, N.C., on Oct. 20. KENT NISHIMURA via Getty Images To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle. At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 60.4% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 37% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -23.4% — near his all-time low. Here's a sampling of Trump's latest net approval numbers from a few top pollsters: New York Times/Siena University : -26% American Research Group : -38% CNN/SSRS : -35% Reuters/Ipsos : -35% Again, history can provide perspective . In late-October 2018, Trump was about 10 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November. According to the New York Times , Trump has the second lowest approval rating heading into the midterms since 1946, behind only Harry Truman. George W. Bush's approval rating was higher at this point in 2006 — a year in which Democrats went on to flip the House and Senate. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 71% disapprove and 25% approve. That's a 46-point gap. In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection. Advantage? Democrats. item.title: Judge tosses new charges against ex-FBI officials in Hunter Biden case and criticizes DOJ
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — A federal magistrate judge on Tuesday rejected the Justice Department's 11th-hour attempt to file new criminal charges against two former FBI counterintelligence officials, saying prosecutors could not take that step without judicial review first. In a tense exchange, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia expressed shock and anger at the Justice Department for filing an unsworn and unsigned superseding complaint against the two FBI officials after midnight on Tuesday on the public court docket, noting it was never reviewed by him to establish whether there was probable cause a crime was committed. Filing an unsworn complaint on the public docket and bypassing judicial review, he said, is unheard of and raises questions about the DOJ's motivations. He said he would be ordering that the new version of the charging documents be "struck from the record," though the Justice Department could try to add new charges the proper way. The docket was later updated to say that the Justice Department's filings were entered "in error." "We have never had complaints filed that are unsigned," Faruqui said. "It is inappropriate. It harms the defendants." "I am unaware of that ever happening before in this court," he added. "I am frustrated that I got it in the middle of the night. But I am much more concerned that it is filed on the public record." John Borchert, a prosecutor from the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C., conceded that the effort by the government to add fresh charges without judicial review in a criminal complaint was a first for him as well. He asked if Faruqui would agree to let the FBI agent who filed the affidavit in support of the new complaint swear and attest to his filing and then proceed with a hearing to determine if probable cause was met. Defense attorneys for the two ex-officials balked, with one calling such a move "Kafkaesque" and Faruqui analogizing such an action to simply serving as a notary. Faruqui accused the government of repeatedly making bizarre moves in the case that only raise concerns, saying it was like throwing gasoline on a fire, citing how the case was charged and the decision to use a special assistant U.S. attorney from out of town to help prosecute the case. "Everything you're doing is making me more and more concerned," he said. "Why today on this one case have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases? It makes it look like the United States is afraid of me trying to find probable cause." "Let me address that squarely. We are not afraid of a probable cause finding," Borchert said. Faruqui said that while he was dismissing the superseding complaint with the new charge of obstructing a congressional proceeding, the court would still proceed with a preliminary hearing to determine whether the original criminal complaint charging them with lying to Congress , which was reviewed by a magistrate judge, meets the probable cause standard. Mary Dohrmann, one of Floris' attorneys, told the court that the changes between the original complaint and the new one the government tried to file were substantial and raised concerns about accuracy. "The evidence is mounting that this prosecution is about some political football, and not the law or the facts in this case," she said. Criminal complaints in felony cases are typically reserved for more exigent circumstances, such as ongoing threats to public safety or national security. And Justice Department guidelines and norms have typically urged prosecutors to avoid taking overt investigative steps on politically sensitive cases so close to a national election. Prosecutors filing an unsworn and unsigned superseding complaint overnight is likely to raise further questions about whether the case is politically motivated. "What is going on at the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office? In the middle of the night, the government filed an unsigned and unsworn complaint attempting to fix the issues with their original charge against Ms. Floris and adding a new charge just as meritless as the first one," said Floris' legal team in a statement provided to CBS News. "In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed," the lawyers said. "That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself. Here, the government has taken that power for itself in a desperate attempt to delay our client's right to challenge the charges in court and litigate this case in the media, rather than the courtroom. We have asked to address this outrageous government conduct against a decorated public servant at today's court hearing." The allegations against Floris and Benavides The charges center on testimony that Floris and Benavides gave a congressional committee on July 19, 2023 and September 28, 2023, respectively. The superseding complaint alleges the defendants "knowingly and willfully provided materially false statements to the Committee about their respective awareness of and involvement in the FBI's investigations into Hunter Biden, and thereby corruptly obstructed, and impeded and endeavored to influence, obstruct, and impede the due proper administration of the law." The complaint is focused on statements they made in testimony concerning their roles on the Foreign Influence Task Force, and one of its counterintelligence operations known as "Round River," which was focused on collecting derogatory informant reporting on, among other things, Hunter Biden, to flag the reporting as Russian disinformation ahead of the 2020 election. Floris served as the deputy assistant director of the FITF from mid-2019 through mid-2022, while Benavides served as its section chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election The complaint alleges that the defendants made false statements in their testimony "for the purpose of minimizing or concealing FITF's engagement with, and communications about, the Hunter Biden investigations and to impede the Congressional investigation." During the hearing, Ron Safer, an attorney for Benavides, cross-examined FBI special agent Bryan Witt over his communications with the House Judiciary Committee. Safer asked how he determined whether Benavides' alleged false statements were material to the committee's investigation and could have affected its decision-making. Witt acknowledged that the FBI was not permitted to directly question committee members or their staff, and that agents instead were required to submit written questions for the record — a method he said he had not experienced before in his career. He added that he had only interviewed Steve Castor, the general counsel for House Judiciary Committee Republicans, a day before Tuesday's hearing. "Nobody would know from reading that affidavit that you were limited in any way in your ability to question the staffers about materiality," Safer said. Prosecutors later told the judge that the FBI was limited in its interactions with the committee because of the Constitution's Speech and Debate clause, which insulates the legislative branch's deliberative process from the executive branch. When Safer pressed Witt further about the conversation with Castor and the written responses from the staffers, Witt admitted that Castor was not present for Benavides' testimony, nor had he reviewed the transcript. Witt also acknowledged that the staffers who reviewed the questions from the FBI were no longer with the committee, and he did not know if they had reviewed the transcript either. The hearing is expected to continue on Wednesday. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/hunter-biden-investigation-more-charges-filed-against-ex-fbi-officials/

item.title: Alex Pretti's family says the DOJ is stonewalling their efforts for justice
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Michael Pretti and Susan Pretti, parents of Alex Pretti, who was killed by federal immigration agents in January, listen during a news conference, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, in Minneapolis. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt) - Ellen Schmidt/AP PROGRAMMING NOTE: Susan and Michael Pretti join CNN’s Jake Tapper on The Lead at 5 p.m. Eastern The parents of Alex Pretti , a US citizen shot and killed by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, are accusing the Department of Justice of violating their rights under a federal victims’ rights law, as they demand transparency and justice in their son’s death. In a July letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche — obtained exclusively by CNN — an attorney representing Michael and Susan Pretti wrote they have not received any substantive updates from the DOJ regarding an investigation into their son’s death, and called the department’s attitude toward the case “cruel.” “The government’s pattern of conduct is not only unconscionable, but unlawful,” the letter states. Pretti’s parents on Tuesday accused the federal government of “shielding Alex’s killers” by not turning over the entire federal case file to state investigators. “We will no longer stay silent about the actions of the Department of Justice in the 275 days since Alex’s murder,” Pretti’s father, Michael, said in the family’s first news conference since the 37-year-old ICU nurse’s death. The Pretti family met with US Attorney for the District of Minnesota Dan Rosen on July 13, the letter explains, the same day Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced in a news conference federal officials had handed over volumes of evidence from Pretti’s shooting. However, the letter goes on to say that, despite a public acknowledgment from local officials of an evidence-sharing agreement, Rosen refused to provide any information and would not even confirm the arrangement. A gunshot perforation in a window pane can be seen in a window in front of a makeshift memorial for Alex Pretti on January 26 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. - Roberto Schmidt/AFP via Getty Images “It is impossible to convey how the government’s refusal to engage in transparent communication with the Pretti family has compounded their heartbreak,” the missive says. “Further, with each such refusal, U.S. Attorney Rosen even refused to explain the basis for his position, instead stating only that ‘I can’t tell you for all kinds of reasons,’ without providing a single one,” according to the letter. Federal investigators who briefly agreed to share their evidence with state law enforcement have since stopped cooperating , said Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, who is leading a lawsuit against the Department of Justice. “We are in litigation with the federal government right now to secure the rest of the remaining file, which they could give us this morning if they were inclined to do so, but it looks like we’re going to need a court order. I’m sorry that it comes to that,” Ellison told CNN’s Sara Sidner Tuesday morning. “Any prosecutor can tell you, you can’t go forward with half a file. You need the whole thing.” CNN has reached out to the DOJ and the US Attorney for Minnesota. In its response to Minnesota’s lawsuit, the Department of Justice said it is not required to turn over evidence to a state agency before an active court case is underway. The Pretti family’s attorney, Steve Schleicher, says they have heard nothing from the DOJ since sending their letter. “I’ve never seen a family treated with such cruelty and disrespect,” he said. Pretti’s death was captured in its entirety on video. Like some other incidents that occurred as a result of the Trump administration’s ongoing immigration crackdown, the footage from Pretti’s shooting differed from the version of events provided by the Department of Homeland Security. unknown content item - Kristi Noem, then-DHS secretary, initially described Pretti as a “terrorist” who “attacked” officers after “brandishing” a weapon, though the video disputed those claims. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller referred to Pretti as an “assassin” who tried to murder federal agents. “No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex,” Michael Pretti said Tuesday. Video footage shows, minutes before the fatal encounter with Pretti, immigration agents patrolling a Minneapolis street and interacting with bystanders. A witness, Nilson Barahona, told CNN agents were trying to apprehend someone who fled into a donut shop that locked its doors, leaving the group of federal officers on the sidewalk and street. Agents detained one observer as others blew whistles, yelled and recorded video on their phones. Video shows Pretti attempting to intervene in a scuffle between an observer and the agents. During the incident, Pretti was pepper-sprayed in the face. One of the officers can be heard in the footage shouting: “Gun! Gun! Gun!” as Pretti is on his knees and bent forward. An agent removed Pretti’s gun from his waistband and can be seen exiting the skirmish. At about the same time, one agent drew his service weapon. About a second after the agent holding Pretti’s weapon moved away, the officer who drew his own weapon appeared to fire several shots at Pretti before another agent drew his weapon and a shot rang out. The other officer then raised his gun and fired more shots. At least 10 gunshots can be heard on the video. The DHS report on its initial investigation into Pretti’s death says an officer yelled, “He’s got a gun” multiple times before the officers fired. “It’s difficult to get up every day, to function, to be a parent, knowing that your child’s never coming home,” Susan Pretti told CNN’s Jake Tapper after Tuesday’s news conference. “No parent should have to live what we’re living. No daughter should have to wake up and know that her only sibling is no longer here.” “What the federal government has taken away from us, from his friends, his family, his colleagues, from his patients, from the patients’ families. They’ve taken away all of that — and it’s reprehensible,” he told Tapper. Susan Pretti said she knew Alex as her son, but the outpouring of support they’ve received from his friends and coworkers has helped her see another side of him. “Every letter and card that we received from his colleagues, telling us who he was, at work … not only helping his patients but his colleagues,” Susan Pretti said, choking up. “You know what that’s like for a parent to hear? It is probably the kindest thing a parent can ever hear about their child.” unknown content item - Michael Pretti said his trust in the government is fading. Pretti’s death followed the fatal shooting of Renee Good on January 7 and the non-fatal shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis on January 14 by immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge. Those incidents prompted significant protests in Minneapolis and across the country for weeks. Hennepin County prosecutors have fought the DOJ for key evidence in Pretti’s death for months, after federal law enforcement repeatedly threw up blockades to their access. On the day Pretti was killed, the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension attempted to access the scene to launch an investigation but was banned by federal authorities. CNN was on scene the next day when the BCA first accessed the scene on a court order from a state judge. item.title: Trump could set off a Senate showdown if a Democrat wins in Alaska
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Senators are bracing for a potential floor fight over accepting the results of the Alaska Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) — and perhaps other battleground contests — if President Trump urges allies to dispute what he might view as unfair or “rigged” results. Democratic senators generally view Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) as a straight shooter who would be averse to rejecting an election result in an Alaska Senate race certified by the governor and lieutenant governor. But they aren’t ruling out the possibility that the president will prod his MAGA allies in the Senate to contest the election results if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses by a narrow margin and blames his loss on voter confusion leading to a significant number of votes for his opponent with a similar name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. If Alaska’s top officials certify Peltola as the winner, and Trump calls on Senate allies to reject that finding, it puts Thune in a tough spot and potentially sets up a messy floor fight. “Everybody is gaming everything out, and everybody is preparing for everything,” a Senate Democratic aide said of the preparations for potential Republican objections if Peltola narrowly beats the incumbent Republican senator. Sarah Binder, a professor of political science at George Washington University and a Senate rules expert, said Trump’s aggressive threat to challenge a Democratic win in Alaska could lead to a nasty Senate floor fight. “We can’t rule anything out at this stage just given the president’s single-minded persistence that there’s a lot of electoral fraud conducted by Democrats,” she said. “Would he push Republicans to object to the seating, if Alaska certified the seating of Peltola? The second question is, if he did that, would Republicans actually follow through?” Binder continued. “That gets us into the hornet’s nest of what the Senate would do to challenge a literal swearing in,” she added. “There’s no single charted pathway here.” She noted that, historically, if Alaska certifies Peltola as the winner over Sen. Dan Sullivan, Republicans could object to swearing her in. “I could imagine a scenario where they would want to swear her in, and somebody objects,” she said. Senate sources familiar with how the floor process would play out said that a Trump-allied senator or a group of GOP senators could signal an intention to object to Peltola — or to the Democratic winner of another close Senate race where Trump might claim election fraud — taking the oath of office to become senator in 2027. That would then lead to a negotiation between Thune and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) over how to resolve the situation. Senate Republican sources say they’re confident that incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan will defeat Peltola next week. Recent polls show Peltola leading the GOP senator by 2 percentage points, but the race is within the margin of error. Recent surveys by Data for Progress, InsiderAdvantage and Alaska Survey Research showed the Democrat leading by 2 points while a New York Times/Siena poll conducted from Sept. 24 to Oct. 1 showed her ahead of Sullivan by 7 points. Alaska has ranked-choice voting, which could shift how some votes are counted. One relevant Senate precedent comes from January 1997, when Republican candidate Woody Jenkins petitioned the Senate to throw out Democrat Mary Landrieu’s victory in the 1996 Senate race in Louisiana. Landrieu won by more than 5,000 votes, but Jenkins alleged “widespread vote tampering.” Senate leaders resolved the matter by agreeing to seat Landrieu “without prejudice” and referring the allegations of election fraud to the Senate Rules Committee to investigate. The deal left open the door to the Senate voting to unseat Landrieu by a majority vote if the charges of cheating were substantiated. In the end, the Rules Committee voted unanimously in October 1997 to end its investigation and clear Landrieu of wrongdoing even though it acknowledged some voting irregularities. Trump is laying the groundwork for a similar fight this fall if Peltola wins, giving Democrats a crucial pickup in a GOP-leaning state. The Trump Justice Department last week asked a federal court to block the certification of the winner of the Alaska Senate race if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses by a narrow margin and could argue that he would have won if his near-namesake, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., hadn’t been on the ballot. Legal experts have broadly dismissed the Justice Department lawsuit as meritless, raising the prospect that Trump’s next move may be to demand that GOP senators refuse to seat Peltola if she wins by a small margin. “They’ve set up the argument already that there’s a deliberate deception on the part of the other Dan Sullivan, and even though this seems to have been adjudicated in Alaska law, they will certainly argue the issue of fairness remains,” said Steven S. Smith, a professor of political science at Arizona State University, who follows Senate politics. Alaska’s Division of Elections, which is led by the state’s Republican lieutenant governor, initially removed “Dan J. Sullivan” from the ballot, but a state judge later ruled that he be placed back on the ballot. The Alaska Supreme Court upheld that decision . To avoid confusion, the Alaska ballot lists “Dan S. Sullivan” as the Republican incumbent and lists his opponent as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” without party affiliation. Given that the Alaska Supreme Court has already ruled that the little-known Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. deserves a spot on the ballot, it would be hard to see how state officials could withhold the certification of a narrow Peltola victory without being overturned by the courts, legal experts say. That then sets the stage for a fight in the Senate, where any number of Trump allies or ambitious Republican senators who are looking for a springboard for national publicity could object to seating Peltola. “This is really a question of Trump-backed Republicans, and I think with Trump probably urging them to exploit every opening, the certification of the Democrat will lead to a Republican challenge if they’re in a position in the Senate to do so,” Smith said. If Peltola wins her race by a narrow margin, however, she will need Alaska’s Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, who handles the duties of the secretary of State, to certify her victory. If Republican state officials refuse to certify a Peltola victory, then Senate Republicans argue the Senate rules would not allow the upper chamber to seat her when the Senate convenes for the new Congress on Jan. 3. The matter would need to be resolved by Alaska’s courts. A similar stalemate played out in 2009 after the close contest between Democrat Al Franken and GOP Sen. Norm Coleman in Minnesota. The state’s Republican Gov. Tim Pawlenty signed the election certificate validating Franken’s victory only after the Minnesota Supreme Court unanimously ruled in June 2009 that Franken had won the race by just more than 200 votes. item.title: Supreme Court declines to restore judges' power to pause deportation cases
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Andrew Chung Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump's administration and Republican-governed Texas ‌that bars the once-common practice. The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities including Baltimore and an immigrant legal ‌advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as "administrative closure," while litigation continues in the dispute. The Supreme Court's decision, issued as a brief, ​one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from decision. The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day. Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal ‌government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the ⁠rule's invalidation. Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as ⁠on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction. Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty. Administrative closure has been applied over the years in ​hundreds ​of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump's ​hardline approach toward immigrants. In 2024, Biden's administration adopted a ‌regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a prior rule adopted in 2020 during Trump's first term in office that had been judicially blocked. After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department office that oversees immigration courts, the Executive Office for Immigration Review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge. In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges "effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens ‌illegally present in this country." Trump's administration and the state then jointly asked ​US District Judge Reed O'Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement ​declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O'Connor did so, blocking it ​permanently, nationwide. Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider, Centro Legal ‌de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case ​to defend the rule, but O'Connor ​rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations. The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O'Connor's decision. The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told ​the Supreme Court in a filing that ‌Trump's administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using "manufactured litigation" with "ideologically aligned" Texas to eliminate a regulation ​it disliked. "The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception," they ​wrote. item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Ricardo Brito and Gram Slattery SAO PAULO, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after losing Sunday's presidential election and refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to hand ‌over his passports, two sources said. The US Embassy in Brazil did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Bolsonaro's ‌lawyer also did not respond. It was not immediately clear where Bolsonaro was heading, what time he would arrive or whether he would seek asylum. US President Donald Trump's ​administration has previously alleged Flavio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil. Flavio's departure for the United States threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaros to put them back in power, and Reuters reported ahead of Sunday's election on a US State Department campaign ‌to restore them to office. Trump made no mention ⁠of Bolsonaro's departure in comments to the press on Monday, but said the Brazilian vote "looked like another rigged election." Lula's office did not respond to a request for comment. Bolsonaro was favored to win Sunday's presidential election ⁠but ended up losing in a shock result to Lula. On Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing, but his documents were cancelled after the deadline lapsed, two other sources said. Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from ​prosecution ​when his Senate term ends in February, said on Monday he had no ​plans to flee. "I have never thought about leaving the ‌country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me." Brazil's Minister of Institutional Relations Jose Guimaraes commented on reports of Bolsonaro leaving the country in an interview with CNN Brasil. "I have no confirmation from the Federal Police or oversight bodies," he told the news outlet. "But this speaks a lot about our opponent’s lack of preparation to govern the country." FOLLOWING FATHER'S PATH Jair Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former US ‌President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned to Brazil but was ​later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed ​government buildings in Brasilia. His son has yet to officially concede ​defeat — saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities — but his ‌Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula's victory. It ​remains unclear how Bolsonaro was able ​to leave the country while he was facing a 24-hour deadline to hand over his passports. A senior Federal Police official said Bolsonaro had not exited the country via any regular migration point. Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro's younger brother who lives in the United ​States, said ahead of the vote that ‌an election loss would require a move. "If my brother does not win, I'm in favor that he would leave the ​country," he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month. item.title: Trump-backed senator warns Republicans could lose the Senate over 1 state
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WICHITA, Kan. — Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., knows that he’s running for his political life, even in deep-red Kansas, where a Democrat hasn’t won since the Great Depression. It’s a Senate race that, until just a few months ago, was not on national Republicans’ radar. But Adam Hamilton, a well-known megachurch pastor styling himself as a moderate, has made the race uncomfortably close for Marshall and the GOP and pushed what was once a safe bet into toss-up territory. In an interview with Fox News Digital in Wichita, Kan., hours before President Donald Trump was set to rally behind the embattled incumbent, Marshall acknowledged that if he falls, Democrats may very well gain control of the Senate. Sleeper Senate Race Emerges As Unexpected Headache For Republicans Ahead Of Midterms President Donald Trump and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., attend a campaign event in Park City, Kansas, on Oct. 19, 2026. "I think that, you know, I'm not a political expert, I'm a physician, but if we lose Kansas, I don't see how we keep control of the Senate," Marshall said. "And that's why a vote for Adam Hamilton is a vote for Chuck Schumer and Democrat control of the Senate. It’s that simple." Republicans are trying to maintain, and even grow, their slim, 53-seat majority in the upper chamber. Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, wasn’t supposed to be a problem. Read On The Fox News App But political experts on the ground contend that Hamilton’s uniqueness as a candidate — he’s been a prominent figure in Kansas for roughly three decades leading the massive Church of the Resurrection — and the political headwinds associated with Trump have created an ideal environment for Marshall to lose. "I can't imagine how factors could be any better for Democrats than they are this election cycle," Don Haider-Markel, a professor of political science at the University of Kansas, told Fox News Digital. "The last time it seemed to be close at all was 2020, and that race ended up not being as close." Dem Senate Hopeful Rejects Schumer But Benefits From Millions In Spending By His Allies That was Marshall’s first race for the Senate, where he won by nearly 12 points with Trump at the top of the ticket. But as Haider-Markel and others have pointed out, midterm elections are typically a check on the party in power, and Trump is not on the ballot this year, though that’s a reality he implored Kansans to ignore during his rally in Park City, Kansas. "In this election, I'm asking you to pretend please that I'm on the ballot," Trump said. "Just pretend." Still, voters in Kansas are dealing with affordability issues and high fuel prices , a point that Marshall admitted was why his race was much closer than outside observers initially predicted. "Look, it's the price of gas, and I do feel people's pain," Marshall said. "Every year I go to all 105 counties, finish up the 105 counties in June, and as that price of gas went up, I felt more and more frustration." "So maybe we're up 12 points before the Iran war, and as the price went up our poll numbers went down, so I think it's the price of gas," he continued. Along the asphalt and concrete arteries that connect Hamilton’s home base of Overland Park, Kansas, to what would be, for a brief moment, the center of the MAGA universe in Wichita, neon signs sprouting from gas stations almost all showed fuel prices that hovered just below $4 for gas and well over $6 for diesel . Trump Voters Reveal Their Biggest Fear Heading Into Midterms — And It's Not Rising Prices Democrat senatorial candidate Adam Hamilton answers questions from the media after a televised debate with Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., at WDAF studios in Kansas City, Mo. Nathaniel Birkhead, a professor of political science at Kansas State University, argued that high gas and diesel prices were certainly a contributing factor to Marshall’s struggles, but not the only one. Birkhead told Fox News Digital that it was Marshall’s tight connection to Trump at a time when the "Trump Brand is not particularly popular" has left an opening for a Democrat like Hamilton to enter the fray. "So we have this kind of contrast of Hamilton benefiting from kind of a down year for Republicans. But then also, again, the fact that Marshall is really kind of tying himself to Trump rather than trying to kind of separate himself," Birkhead said. "I think if this had been Jerry Moran running instead of Roger Marshall, I think it'd be far less competitive." Click Here To Download The Fox News App Therein lies the conundrum for Marshall and Republicans — they know that they need Trump’s support and his loyal base of voters, but they have to walk a fine line to capture other Republican voters and independents that might sit this election out or vote the other way. And that’s the crux of Marshall’s argument: without MAGA voters, he can’t win. "Look, I'm the doctor always weighing the benefits and risks of everything. And I'm telling you, we don't win this election without Trump voters getting out and voting," Marshall said. "The majority of the undecideds are Trump supporters. And they need to hear from him, 'Here's the plan, and this is how we're going to bring those prices back down, that if we leave Democrats in control, the price of the gas will never go down.'" item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump took seven minutes out of his Monday night rally in Corinth, Mississippi, to defend his focus on White House renovation projects after one of his predecessors, Barack Obama, compared the redecorated Oval Office to an over-the-top Cheesecake Factory. Trump denied spending excessive time on the projects, then went on to detail repairs to exterior plaster, as well as construction of a heliport and ballroom. He described the executive mansion's previous condition in dire terms, including a cracked column, missing ornamentation and broken tile. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. "I fix things very good, very beautifully," he said. "It's a natural thing. It actually relaxes me." Obama, campaigning for Democrats in Ohio on Saturday, joked that the proliferation of gold-colored appliqués in Trump's Oval Office looked "like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory." With his focus on home renovations, Obama added, Trump "should be on HGTV." The slight played on a broader vulnerability for Trump, a real estate developer by profession, who has devoted considerable attention to remaking the White House and Washington even as most Americans disapprove of the projects. Fifty-nine percent of respondents to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll conducted this month said Trump was spending "too much" time on the projects, compared with 27 percent of adults who said he is spending the right amount of time on the projects and 11 percent who said not enough. Obama's criticism appeared to particularly rankle Trump, who has feuded with him for decades. Trump on Monday praised the Cheesecake Factory as "a very successful company" and defended the importance of tending to the White House's physical condition. "The White House represents our country, and that has to be pristine," he said. "And I would try and explain that to a guy like Obama, but he wouldn't understand." Trump said he noticed the building in disrepair during a visit 20 years ago. There is no record of Trump visiting the White House between 1987, at a reception with President Ronald Reagan, and 2016, after he won the November presidential election. Trump said he would have done the renovations in his first term but didn't have the time. He then again denied spending time on them. "I didn't take any time," he said. "It's been my honor to do it.
